narrative.text: Summarizes the TB-LAMP policy guidance, explaining the End TB Strategy's call for early diagnosis and how the manual LAMP assay works and can be read under ultraviolet light. It recounts the 2012 Guideline Development Group review and the newer evidence assessment. It then states the conditional recommendations for using TB-LAMP instead of, or after, sputum-smear microscopy, together with remarks limiting their scope.

Sets out the background to TB-LAMP, noting that a large share of TB cases worldwide go undetected and that new diagnostics are a priority. It describes the commercial Eiken assay, its modest infrastructure needs and its history of WHO review. It then walks through the TB-LAMP workflow, from sample preparation and heating to visual reading of fluorescence and waste disposal.

Explains that the GRADE approach and PICO-framed questions were used to assess the evidence on TB-LAMP. It lists the four review questions on accuracy versus microscopy, use as an add-on test, comparison with Xpert MTB/RIF, and rates of invalid results.

Defines which TB-LAMP studies were eligible for the systematic review, including prospective studies after 2012 in intermediate- and high-burden settings and a supplementary literature search. It lists exclusion criteria for studies and individual participants and describes the culture-based reference standards and smear microscopy definitions used.

Describes how individual-level data were obtained from FIND-affiliated and other TB-LAMP studies, listing the minimum and optional variables collected. It then outlines how accuracy, incremental yield and invalid result rates were calculated and how heterogeneity was assessed.
Notes that a WHO Guideline Development Group met in January 2016 to review 20 new TB-LAMP studies, 13 of which met inclusion criteria, and outlines the roles of the methodologist and Steering Group.

Describes how the Steering Group handled interests, PICO questions and the consensus process for the TB-LAMP recommendations, and how an External Review Group of laboratory experts found no major errors or concerns in the guidance.
States that the guidance summarizes evidence and recommendations on using TB-LAMP for pulmonary TB in symptomatic adults and should be read with WHO's 2015 framework for implementing TB diagnostics.
Identifies the intended users of the TB-LAMP guidance, from clinicians and laboratory directors to donors, procurement officers and programme planners.

Describes the evidence base for the TB-LAMP recommendations: of 20 studies identified, 13 in 11 countries met inclusion criteria, many of them unpublished. It explains the role of FIND in conducting or sponsoring most studies and gives participant numbers and study periods. Tables summarize study characteristics such as setting, HIV prevalence and reference standards.

Reports the QUADAS-2 appraisal of the included TB-LAMP studies, judging overall risk of bias as high mainly because of the culture reference standard, unclear patient selection and flow and timing problems. A table gives each study's risk-of-bias and applicability ratings, and notes explain the judgements.

Presents the accuracy of TB-LAMP as a replacement for smear microscopy, with the numbers of eligible and included participants by study and reference standard. Forest plots and pooled sensitivity and specificity estimates are given for each of the three culture-based standards. Table notes define the standards used.

Reports the limited data on TB-LAMP accuracy among adults living with HIV, giving the ranges of sensitivity and specificity across studies for each reference standard. It notes greater heterogeneity and provides pooled estimates in a table.

Presents the accuracy of TB-LAMP as an add-on test for adults with two negative smear results, with participant numbers by study and reference standard. Pooled sensitivity and specificity for smear-negative, culture-positive TB are shown with forest plots. Table notes define the culture standards.

Compares the diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP and the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in participants tested with both, giving numbers of included participants by study. Pooled sensitivity and specificity for each test and their differences are presented across three reference standards.
Reports that indeterminate or invalid TB-LAMP results were rare, with a pooled proportion of about zero among all adults and among those with HIV.

Summarizes a costing study of TB-LAMP and Xpert MTB/RIF in peripheral laboratories in Malawi and Viet Nam, comparing TB-LAMP strategies with microscopy-based care. It gives per-test costs and affordability and cost-effectiveness findings, and cautions policy-makers to weigh feasibility and costs before adoption.
Introduces the evidence-to-recommendation summary, noting that TB-LAMP accuracy on sputum was determined from 13 studies in intermediate- and high-burden countries.

Explains the Guideline Development Group's reasoning on TB-LAMP for all adults: higher sensitivity than microscopy with slightly lower specificity, partly attributed to culture misclassification. It weighs the extra cases detected per 1 000 tested against false positives and concludes the trade-off is acceptable.

Reports that in a small HIV-positive group TB-LAMP performed about the same as smear microscopy, and explains why the group made no specific recommendation for people living with HIV, citing limited evidence.

Sets out the reasoning for TB-LAMP as an add-on test after negative smear microscopy, citing a 42% incremental yield and slightly lower specificity. It concludes that more cases would be found with an acceptable number of false positives.

Compares TB-LAMP with Xpert MTB/RIF, noting lower sensitivity and no rifampicin resistance detection, and explains why Xpert remains preferred where resources allow while TB-LAMP may suit peripheral sites.

States WHO's two conditional recommendations, based on very low-quality evidence, for TB-LAMP as a replacement for or follow-on to smear microscopy in symptomatic adults. Remarks restrict their use to sputum, caution against replacing rapid rifampicin-resistance tests and note uncertainty for people with HIV and extrapolation to children.

Lists implementation considerations for TB-LAMP, including electricity, storage temperature, waste disposal and stock needs. It also notes that smear microscopy is still needed for treatment monitoring and that Xpert MTB/RIF should not be replaced.
Describes how the TB-LAMP guidance will be published online and distributed to WHO offices, Member States and partner networks.
Lists research needs for TB-LAMP, such as studies with stronger culture reference standards, evaluation of diagnostic algorithms, training needs, patient impact and country-specific cost analyses.
A reference list of the studies included in, and excluded from, the systematic review of TB-LAMP diagnostic accuracy, many unpublished or submitted for publication.

Presents GRADE evidence profiles comparing TB-LAMP with sputum-smear microscopy for diagnosing pulmonary TB in adults, against a culture reference standard. Tables give pooled sensitivity and specificity and the expected true and false positives and negatives per 1000 patients at different pre-test probabilities. Footnotes explain why the evidence was rated very low or low quality, citing risk of bias, indirectness and heterogeneity across studies.

Reproduces abstracts of unpublished studies on TB-LAMP included in the review, beginning with a Côte d'Ivoire study comparing smear microscopy, TB-LAMP and GeneXpert MTB/RIF against liquid culture in symptomatic patients. Each abstract outlines background, methods, sample sizes and the sensitivity and specificity results obtained. The section ends with WHO Global TB Programme contact details.

The front matter of WHO policy guidance on using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) to diagnose pulmonary tuberculosis. It includes the cover, cataloguing data with ISBN, copyright and disclaimer notices, and a table of contents covering methods, results of the systematic review, cost-effectiveness and recommendations. It also contains acknowledgements and lists of contributors. It ends with the declarations of interest of Guideline Development Group members and the planned review date of 2020.
